newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Coffee-Swiss trade differs on 97/98 Brazil crop.
newsitem.headline: Coffee-Swiss trade differs on 97/98 Brazil crop.

text.p: Brazil's coffee harvest could exceed 30 million 60-kg bags in 1997/98 crop, up from around 27 million in 1996/97, several major Swiss traders predicted.
This would be a sharp jump from the weather-hit crop of 12.5 million in 1995/96, they said.
Brazil is the world's top coffee grower and analysts said its crop development would be a key price factor in the coming weeks.
Other traders said while it was still early to gauge the 1997/98 output, a figure above 30 million may be pure guesswork.
But they were unwilling to consider a recent suggestion from a Brazilian coffee growers' association in Cerrado, Minas Gerais (Caccer) that the crop could fall to 17.8 million.
"I see a crop of 26 million bags this season. After that, a bumper crop will be a surprise, but talk of 17-18 million is rubbish," one said.
Caccer predicted such a low crop on the basis that it is the off-year in Brazil's bi-annual growing cycle.
The size of the 1997/98 Brazilian crop remains the main talking point among the coffee community in Switzerland, home to some of the largest roasters and traders.
Even the 1996/97 crop remains an issue, with the traders estimating the yield at between 26 million and 30 million.
"Brazil will have more than 27 million bags in 1996/97," a trader at a leading trade house said. "In 1997/98, the crop could reach over 30 million."
Assuming that Brazilian output exceeds 30 million bags, then the world coffee balance will see a surplus of five to six million against a neutral to one million deficit this season.
The trader said there had been favourable weather in Brazilian coffee regions in October and November, the crucial time for flowering.
"There's a very good (crop) potential for next year and by January, the market will talking 30 million bags," he said.
Another Swiss trader said: "This year, it will be about 29-30 million and the next one will be at least 30 million."
"But at 30 million, it is not huge, just a normal crop. I think Brazil has the potential by the next three crops to produce over 35 million."
He said many coffee areas, hit by frosts and a drought in 1994, had been replanted with higher-yielding trees.
"These trees may start producing in 1997 but they will not reach full production until 1998/99," he said.

The higher production will also hinge on average world prices staying above 80 U.S. cents a lb. The average cost of production is 80-90 cents worldwide and in the case of Brazil, the cost is around 70 cents.
"Under 80 cents, farmers will lose motivation," one said.
A trader at one large European roaster said: "What I have heard is 32-35 million bags in 1997/98 for Brazil against 26-28 million this season.
Commodity brokers GNI said this week its 1996/97 estimate for Brazil of 27 million bags had some scope for downward revisions later in the year.
It gave no forecast for the next crop saying that it was difficult to draw conclusions just yet from initially poor flowerings.
"Any 'reliable' forecast calling for a sub-28 million bag crop should be viewed positively," GNI said.
GNI noted lack of independent crop watchers but said a forecast by a former U.S. Department of Agriculture statistician in Brazil due in the near future would give the market a good feel for 1997/98.
